title: Digital Literacy & Safety
description: Stay safe online: strong passwords, spotting scams, protecting privacy, and checking facts.

stations.title: Strong Passwords
stations.summary: A password is the key to your digital home. Using one key for every door is dangerous.
points: Length beats complexity: 12+ characters (a passphrase) beats 'P@ssw0rd'.
One account, one password. Never reuse your email password on social media.
Turn on two-factor authentication (2FA) for email, social media, and digital wallets.
Use a password manager so you do not have to memorise everything.

questions.prompt: Which of these passwords is strongest?
options: P@ssw0rd
letmein123
MyCatSleepsInsideCardboardBoxes!
questions.explain: A long passphrase is easy to remember but hard for machines to guess. Common patterns like 'P@ssw0rd' are already in cracking dictionaries.

questions.prompt: Why is reusing the same password on every account risky?
options: It uses too much mobile data
One leaked account can unlock all the others
It makes the phone heat up
Every app forbids it
questions.explain: A breach on one site leads to credential stuffing: attackers reuse the same email+password pair elsewhere.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of two-factor authentication (2FA)?
options: To double your internet speed
To add a security layer even if the password leaks
To delete all old passwords
To make an account impossible to hack
questions.explain: 2FA adds a second factor (OTP code or authenticator app). Stay alert though — no system is 100% attack-proof.

cards.back: Long (12+ characters), unique per account, use a passphrase
Second layer: an OTP code or authenticator app

stations.title: Spotting Online Scams
stations.summary: Scammers rarely hack systems — they hack panic and impatience.
points: Beware urgency: 'account will be closed', 'you won a prize', 'transfer right now'.
Check the sender's address, not just its display name.
Never share an OTP code with anyone, including people claiming to be staff.
Distrust short links and unsolicited attachments; open the official app yourself.

questions.prompt: Someone claiming to be from your bank asks for an OTP to 'verify' you. Best response?
options: Give it so the account is not blocked
Refuse and call the bank on its official number
Send only half of the code
Share it in a family group chat to ask
questions.explain: An OTP is the last key to your account. Real bank staff never ask for it by phone or chat.

questions.prompt: A common sign of a phishing message is...
options: Neatly written with no typos
Urgent and asking for personal data
Sent from an official domain
Contains no links at all
questions.explain: Time pressure ('right now', 'within 5 minutes') is used so the victim has no time to think.

questions.prompt: The safest way to open a 'notification' from your bank or a marketplace?
options: Click the link in the message and log in
Open the official app or website yourself
Reply to the message to confirm
Forward it to a friend first
questions.explain: Always travel a road you typed yourself. Links can lead to look-alike sites that are nearly identical.

cards.back: Secret. Never shared with anyone, including 'staff'
Urgent, tempting, or frightening + asks for data or a click

stations.title: Digital Footprints & Privacy
stations.summary: What you share online tends to stay — even after you delete it.
points: A digital footprint is every trace left behind: uploads, comments, location, search history.
Think before sharing photos of your ID card, boarding pass, or home address.
Review app permissions: does a torch app really need your location?
Use privacy settings; not every post has to be public.

options: Only the photos you personally upload
Every trace left behind: uploads, comments, location, search history
Only private messages you deleted
Only data on a work computer
questions.explain: It includes data you leave deliberately and unintentionally, including metadata.

questions.prompt: Which document is riskiest to share on social media?
options: A photo of your ID card
A landscape photo
A recipe
A photo of a plant
questions.explain: Full identity details can be used to open accounts or borrow money in your name.

questions.prompt: Why should app permissions be reviewed?
options: So the battery lasts forever
Because apps can collect more data than they need
Because every app must request location
So updates are no longer necessary
questions.explain: Least-privilege: grant the smallest set of permissions that still makes the app useful.

cards.back: Every trace from online activity, intentional or not
Grant as few permissions as possible

stations.title: Misinformation & Fact-Checking
stations.summary: Fake news spreads on emotion, not evidence. Spend 30 seconds before you share.
points: Read past the headline: hoaxes are often only ever read as headlines.
Check other credible sources — if only one site reports it, be suspicious.
Watch the date: old photos and stories are often recycled as today's news.
Use official fact-checking sites and reverse image search.

questions.prompt: The first step when a shocking story lands in the family group chat is...
options: Share it immediately so others know
Read it fully, then check other sources
Reply with an emoji only
Save it and forget it
questions.explain: Pause and verify. Misinformation is engineered to trigger emotions that make you share instantly.

questions.prompt: A sign that a story may be false is...
options: A named author and clear sources
A sensational headline that provokes anger or fear
Links to official institutions
A complete date for the event
questions.explain: Headlines like 'SHOCKING!' or 'VIRAL' that push you to share right away are a warning sign.

questions.prompt: A disaster photo from 2015 is shared as if it happened today. This is...
options: False context
Valid news
Personal opinion
An advert
questions.explain: The photo is real, the context is fake. Reverse image search helps find the original source.

cards.back: Read to the end · check other sources · check the date
An old photo or story reused for a new event
